claim: Traditional accumulation-to-bound decision-making models assume that all choice options are processed with equal attention.
source: Traditional accumulation-to-bound decision-making models assume that all choice options are processed with equal attention.
evidence: This is a statement about existing models in the literature, supported by citations in the broader context.

claim: In real life decisions, humans alternate their visual fixation between individual items to efficiently gather relevant information.
source: In real life decisions, however, humans alternate their visual fixation between individual items to efficiently gather relevant information (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2016.

claim: Visual fixations causally affect one's choices, biasing them toward the longer-fixated item.
source: These fixations also causally affect one's choices, biasing them toward the longer-fixated item (Krajbich et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krajbich et al., 2010.

claim: Attention enhances the reliability of information, consistent with neurophysiological findings.
source: We derive a normative decision-making model in which attention enhances the reliability of information, consistent with neurophysiological findings (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cohen and Maunsell, 2009.

claim: The optimal model reproduces fixation-related choice biases seen in humans.
source: We show that the optimal model reproduces fixation-related choice biases seen in humans and provides a Bayesian computational rationale for this phenomenon.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The optimal model provides a Bayesian computational rationale for fixation-related choice biases.
source: We show that the optimal model reproduces fixation-related choice biases seen in humans and provides a Bayesian computational rationale for this phenomenon.
evidence: This is a theoretical contribution of the study, supported by the model derivation and Figure 4A.

claim: Decision performance is benefited by a balanced spread of resources between the attended and unattended items.
source: Finally, by varying the relative cognitive advantage conferred by attention, we show that decision performance is benefited by a balanced spread of resources between the attended and unattended items.
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Accumulation-to-bound models have been successful at describing accuracy and response time data from human decision makers in perceptual and value-based decision tasks.
source: Such models have been successful at describing accuracy and response time data from human decision makers performing in both perceptual and value-based decision tasks (Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008; Milosavljevic et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008 and Milosavljevic et al., 2010.

claim: The normative strategy for decision-making can be implemented as an accumulation-to-bound model with time-varying decision boundaries that approach each other over time.
source: Recently, we and others showed that, if we assume these computations to involve a stream of noisy samples of each item's perceptual feature (for perceptual decisions) or underlying value (for value-based decisions), then the normative strategy could be implemented as an accumulation-to-bound model (Bogacz et al., 2006; Drugowitsch et al., 2012; Tajima et al., 2016). Specifically, the normative strategy could be described with the diffusion decision model (Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008) with time-varying decision boundaries that approach each other over time.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bogacz et al., 2006; Drugowitsch et al., 2012; Tajima et al., 2016; and Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008.

claim: Standard accumulation-to-bound models assume that all choice options receive equal attention during decision-making.
source: Standard accumulation-to-bound models assume that all choice options receive equal attention during decision-making.
evidence: This is a statement about existing models in the literature.

claim: Humans tend to alternate between fixating on different items when making decisions.
source: Indeed, humans tend to alternate between fixating on different items when making decisions, suggesting that control of overt visual attention is intrinsic to the decision-making process (Kustov and Robinson, 1996; Mohler and Wurtz, 1976).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kustov and Robinson, 1996 and Mohler and Wurtz, 1976.

claim: Human final choices are biased toward the item that they looked at longer.
source: Furthermore, their final choices are biased toward the item that they looked at longer, a phenomenon referred to as a choice bias (Shimojo et al., 2003; Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Cavanagh et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shimojo et al., 2003; Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Cavanagh et al., 2014.

claim: Prior models assumed that fixations are driven by brain processes that are exogenous to the computations involved in decision-making.
source: For example, the choice bias has been previously replicated with a modified accumulation-to-bound model, but the model assumed that fixations are driven by brain processes that are exogenous to the computations involved in decision-making (Krajbich et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krajbich et al., 2010.

claim: Fixations appear to be controlled to extract choice-relevant information in a statistically efficient manner.
source: This stands in contrast to studies of visual attention where fixations appear to be controlled to extract choice-relevant information in a statistically efficient manner, suggesting that fixations are driven by processes endogenous to the decision (Yang et al., 2016; Hoppe and Rothkopf, 2016; Hayhoe and Ballard, 2005; Chukoskie et al., 2013; Corbetta and Shulman, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 2016; Hoppe and Rothkopf, 2016; Hayhoe and Ballard, 2005; Chukoskie et al., 2013; Corbetta and Shulman, 2002.

claim: Visual attention selectively increases the firing rate of neurons tuned to task-relevant stimuli.
source: Our approach was inspired by neurophysiological findings demonstrating that visual attention selectively increases the firing rate of neurons tuned to task-relevant stimuli (Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004), decreases the mean-normalized variance of individual neurons (Mitchell et al., 2007; Wittig et al., 2018), and reduces the correlated variability of neurons at the population level (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009; Averbeck et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004.

claim: Visual attention decreases the mean-normalized variance of individual neurons.
source: Our approach was inspired by neurophysiological findings demonstrating that visual attention selectively increases the firing rate of neurons tuned to task-relevant stimuli (Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004), decreases the mean-normalized variance of individual neurons (Mitchell et al., 2007; Wittig et al., 2018), and reduces the correlated variability of neurons at the population level (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009; Averbeck et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mitchell et al., 2007 and Wittig et al., 2018.

claim: Visual attention reduces the correlated variability of neurons at the population level.
source: Our approach was inspired by neurophysiological findings demonstrating that visual attention selectively increases the firing rate of neurons tuned to task-relevant stimuli (Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004), decreases the mean-normalized variance of individual neurons (Mitchell et al., 2007; Wittig et al., 2018), and reduces the correlated variability of neurons at the population level (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009; Averbeck et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2009; Averbeck et al., 2006.

claim: The optimal policy switches attention more frequently when deciding between items with similar values.
source: We then show that this strategy featured the same choice bias as observed in human decision makers: it switched attention more frequently when deciding between items with similar values, and was biased toward choosing items that were attended last, and attended longer.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The optimal policy is biased toward choosing items that were attended last.
source: We then show that this strategy featured the same choice bias as observed in human decision makers: it switched attention more frequently when deciding between items with similar values, and was biased toward choosing items that were attended last, and attended longer.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The optimal policy is biased toward choosing items that were attended longer.
source: We then show that this strategy featured the same choice bias as observed in human decision makers: it switched attention more frequently when deciding between items with similar values, and was biased toward choosing items that were attended last, and attended longer.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Choice biases vary based on the amount of time spent on the decision.
source: It furthermore led to new predictions that we could confirm in human behavior: choice biases varied based on the amount of time spent on the decision and the average desirability across both choice items.
evidence: This is a prediction confirmed in human data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Choice biases vary based on the average desirability across both choice items.
source: It furthermore led to new predictions that we could confirm in human behavior: choice biases varied based on the amount of time spent on the decision and the average desirability across both choice items.
evidence: This is a prediction confirmed in human data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The decision maker knows the shape of the prior but can't directly observe the drawn true values.
source: We assume the decision maker knows the shape of the prior, but can't directly observe the drawn true values.
evidence: This is a model assumption.

claim: The posterior belief's variance reflects the uncertainty in the decision maker's value inference.
source: The posterior's variance (i.e. the second fraction in brackets) reflects the uncertainty in the decision maker's value inference.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mathematical model.

claim: Uncertainty monotonically decreases identically over time for both items in the attention-free model.
source: In this attention-free model, uncertainty monotonically decreases identically over time for both items, reflecting the standard assumption of accumulation-to-bound models that, in each small time period, the same amount of evidence is gathered for either choice item.
evidence: This is a property of the attention-free model derived from the equations.

claim: Attention limits information about the unattended item.
source: To introduce attention-modulation, we assume that attention limits information about the unattended item (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a model assumption illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Attention boosts behavioral performance.
source: This is consistent with behavioral and neurophysiological findings showing that attention boosts behavioral performance (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Cohen and Maunsell, 2010; Wang and Krauzlis, 2018) and the information encoded in neural populations (Ni et al., 2018; Ruff et al., 2018; Wittig et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Cohen and Maunsell, 2010; Wang and Krauzlis, 2018.

claim: Attention boosts the information encoded in neural populations.
source: This is consistent with behavioral and neurophysiological findings showing that attention boosts behavioral performance (Cohen and Maunsell, 2009; Cohen and Maunsell, 2010; Wang and Krauzlis, 2018) and the information encoded in neural populations (Ni et al., 2018; Ruff et al., 2018; Wittig et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ni et al., 2018; Ruff et al., 2018; Wittig et al., 2018.

claim: The optimal policy space can be divided into regions associated with different optimal actions.
source: The policy space can be divided into regions associated with different optimal actions (choose item 1 or 2, accumulate more evidence, switch attention).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The two policy spaces for attending to item 1 versus item 2 are mirror-images of each other.
source: The two policy spaces are mirror-images of each other.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The model never switches attention or makes a decision immediately after an attention switch.
source: As expected, the 'switch' region in a given policy space is always encompassed in the 'accumulate' region of the other policy space, indicating that the model never switches attention or makes a decision immediately after an attention switch.
evidence: This is an observation from the optimal policy shown in Figure 2.

claim: The decision boundaries in 3D space approach each other over time.
source: Furthermore, the decision boundaries in 3D space approach each other over time, consistent with previous work that showed a collapsing 2D boundary for optimal value-based decisions without attention (Tajima et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an observation from the optimal policy with citation to Tajima et al., 2016.

claim: The collapsing bound reflects the model's uncertainty regarding the difficulty of the decision task.
source: The collapsing bound reflects the model's uncertainty regarding the difficulty of the decision task (Drugowitsch et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Drugowitsch et al., 2012.

claim: The model replicated a particular fixation pattern seen in humans, where a short first fixation is followed by a significantly longer second fixation, which is followed by a medium-length third fixation.
source: Interestingly, the model also replicated a particular fixation pattern seen in humans, where a short first fixation is followed by a significantly longer second fixation, which is followed by a medium-length third fixation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The attentional drift diffusion model (aDDM) did not generate its own fixations, but rather used fixations sampled from the empirical distribution of human subjects.
source: Of note, the attentional drift diffusion model (aDDM) that was initially proposed to explain the observed human data did not generate its own fixations, but rather used fixations sampled from the empirical distribution of human subjects.
evidence: This is a statement about the aDDM model from Krajbich et al., 2010.

claim: The aDDM was only able to achieve the observed fixation pattern by sampling the first fixation separately from the remaining fixation durations.
source: Furthermore, they were only able to achieve this fixation pattern by sampling the first fixation, which was generally shorter than the rest, separately from the remaining fixation durations (Krajbich et al., 2010; Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is a statement about the aDDM model with citation to Krajbich et al., 2010 and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Attention only modulates the variance of momentary evidence without explicitly down-weighting the value of the unattended item in the current model.
source: One feature that distinguishes our model from previous attention-based decision models is that attention only modulates the variance of momentary evidence without explicitly down-weighting the value of the unattended item (Krajbich et al., 2010; Song et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the model's features with citations to Krajbich et al., 2010 and Song et al., 2019.

claim: Bayesian belief updating with attention modulation effectively accounts for a biasing effect of fixation on the subjective value of items under the assumption of a zero-mean prior.
source: However, under the assumption that decision makers start out with a zero-mean prior, Bayesian belief updating with attention modulation turns out to effectively account for a biasing effect of fixation on the subjective value of items (Li and Ma, 2019).
evidence: This is an inference from the model with citation to Li and Ma, 2019.

claim: Attending to one of two equally-valued items for a longer time leads to a subjectively higher value for the longer attended item.
source: This leads to a higher subjective value of item 1 compared to that of item 2 even though their true underlying values are equal.
evidence: This is an inference from the Bayesian model illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: The aDDM produced qualitatively similar behavioral predictions as the optimal model.
source: Despite this difference, the aDDM produced qualitatively similar behavioral predictions as the optimal model (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and Figure 4—figure supplement 3 for additional behavioral comparisons between human data, the optimal model, and aDDM).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing model simulations shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Fixation can bias choices in a perceptual decision-making paradigm.
source: The impact of attention is not unique to value-based decisions. In fact, recent work showed that fixation can bias choices in a perceptual decision-making paradigm (Tavares et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tavares et al., 2017.

claim: The longer fixated option was more likely to be chosen in the perceptual decision task.
source: Consistent with results in the value-based decision task, the authors demonstrated that the longer fixated option was more likely to be chosen.
evidence: This is a finding from Tavares et al., 2017.

claim: The optimal policy for perceptual decisions was successful at reproducing the attention-driven biases seen in humans.
source: Similar to our value-based case, the optimal policy for perceptual decisions was successful at reproducing the attention-driven biases seen in humans in Tavares et al., 2017, (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 with citation to Tavares et al., 2017.

claim: The current model provides a unified framework in which fixations are endogenously generated as a core component of the normative decision-making strategy.
source: First, we provide a unified framework in which fixations are endogenously generated as a core component of the normative decision-making strategy.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's contribution.

claim: Fixation patterns are influenced by variables relevant for the decision, such as trial difficulty or the value of each choice item.
source: This is consistent with previous work that showed that fixation patterns were influenced by variables relevant for the decision, such as trial difficulty or the value of each choice item (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Krajbich et al., 2010 and Krajbich and Rangel, 2011.

claim: Prior models assumed an exogenous source of fixations.
source: However, prior models of such decisions assumed an exogenous source of fixations (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011) or generated fixations using heuristics that relied on features such as the salience or value estimates of the choice options (Towal et al., 2013; Gluth et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Towal et al., 2013; Gluth et al., 2020.

claim: Some prior models generated fixations using heuristics that relied on features such as the salience or value estimates of the choice options.
source: However, prior models of such decisions assumed an exogenous source of fixations (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011) or generated fixations using heuristics that relied on features such as the salience or value estimates of the choice options (Towal et al., 2013; Gluth et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Towal et al., 2013 and Gluth et al., 2020.

claim: Some models assumed that fixation duration should depend on the expected utility or informativeness of the choice items.
source: Other models generated fixations under the assumption that fixation duration should depend on the expected utility or informativeness of the choice items (Cassey et al., 2013; Ke et al., 2016; Song et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cassey et al., 2013; Ke et al., 2016; Song et al., 2019.

claim: A recent normative model supported a continuous change of attention across choice items, and so could not relate attention to the observed discrete fixation changes.
source: A recent normative model supported a continuous change of attention across choice items, and so could not relate attention to the observed discrete fixation changes (Hébert and Woodford, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hébert and Woodford, 2019.

claim: Fixation patterns could reflect active information gathering through controlling an attentional bottleneck.
source: Our work significantly builds on these prior models by identifying the exact optimal policy using dynamic programming, demonstrating that fixation patterns could reflect active information gathering through controlling an attentional bottleneck.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model analysis.

claim: Previous models accounted for attention by down-weighting the value of the unattended item.
source: In contrast, previous models accounted for attention by down-weighting the value of the unattended item (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Song et al., 2019), where one would a priori assume fixations to bias choices.
evidence: Supported by citations to Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Song et al., 2019.

claim: Selective attention appears to boost the signal-to-noise ratio, or the reliability of information encoded by neuronal signals rather than alter the magnitude of the value encoded by these signals.
source: In essence, selective attention appears to boost the signal-to-noise ratio, or the reliability of information encoded by neuronal signals rather than alter the magnitude of the value encoded by these signals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of neurophysiological findings cited earlier.

claim: The attention-modulated optimal policy can be implemented as a four-dimensional accumulation-to-bound model.
source: Under this framework, we show that the optimal policy can be implemented as a four-dimensional accumulation-to-bound model where the particle drifts and diffuses according to the fixation duration to either item, the currently attended item, and the difference the in items' value estimates.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: The attention-modulated optimal policy still featured a collapsing boundary in time consistent with the attention-free case.
source: Nevertheless, the attention-modulated optimal policy still featured a collapsing boundary in time consistent with the attention-free case (Drugowitsch et al., 2012; Tajima et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an observation from the optimal policy with citations to Drugowitsch et al., 2012 and Tajima et al., 2016.

claim: The aim was to provide a precise, normative explanation for how fixation changes qualitatively interact with human decisions rather than quantitatively capture all details of human behavior.
source: Our aim was to provide a precise (i.e. without approximations), normative explanation for how fixation changes qualitatively interact with human decisions rather than quantitatively capture all details of human behavior, which is likely driven by additional heuristics and features beyond the scope of our model (Acerbi et al., 2014; Drugowitsch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's goals with citations to Acerbi et al., 2014 and Drugowitsch et al., 2016.

claim: It has been suggested that normative allocation of attention should also depend on the item values to eliminate non-contenders.
source: For instance, it has been suggested that normative allocation of attention should also depend on the item values to eliminate non-contenders, which we did not incorporate as a part of our model (Towal et al., 2013; Gluth et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Towal et al., 2013 and Gluth et al., 2020.

claim: Other models using approximations are expected to have a better quantitative fit to human data.
source: As such, we expect other models using approximations to have a better quantitative fit to human data (Krajbich et al., 2010; Callaway et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculation with citations to Krajbich et al., 2010 and Callaway et al., 2020.

claim: The nervous system is expected to implement the optimal policy only approximately due to its complexity.
source: Due to the optimal policy's complexity (Figure 2), we expect the nervous system to implement it only approximately (e.g. similar to Tajima et al., 2019 for multi-alternative decisions).
evidence: This is a speculation with citation to Tajima et al., 2019.

claim: Callaway et al., 2020 proposed a model of N-alternative choice using approaches from rational inattention to approximate optimal decision-making in the presence of an attentional bottleneck.
source: Such an approximation has been recently suggested by Callaway et al., 2020, where they proposed a model of N-alternative choice using approaches from rational inattention to approximate optimal decision-making in the presence of an attentional bottleneck.
evidence: Supported by citation to Callaway et al., 2020.

claim: Callaway et al., 2020 assumed that the unattended item is completely ignored.
source: Unlike our work, they assumed that the unattended item is completely ignored, and therefore could not investigate the effect of graded shifts of attentional resources between items (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a comparison with Callaway et al., 2020.

claim: Callaway et al., 2020's model did not predict a choice bias in binary choices due to a different assumption about the Bayesian prior.
source: In addition, their model did not predict a choice bias in binary choices due to a different assumption about the Bayesian prior.
evidence: This is a comparison with Callaway et al., 2020.

claim: The current model assumed the decision maker's prior belief about the item values is centered at zero.
source: In our model, we assumed the decision maker's prior belief about the item values is centered at zero.
evidence: This is a model assumption.

claim: Callaway et al., 2020 chose a prior distribution based on the choice set, centered on the average value of only the tested items.
source: In contrast, Callaway et al., 2020 chose a prior distribution based on the choice set, centered on the average value of only the tested items.
evidence: This is a comparison with Callaway et al., 2020.

claim: The zero-mean prior predicts an opposite effect of the choice bias when deciding between aversive items, such that less-fixated items should become the preferred choice.
source: The zero-mean prior also predicts an opposite effect of the choice bias when deciding between aversive items, such that less-fixated items should become the preferred choice. This is exactly what has been observed in human decision makers (Armel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model confirmed by citation to Armel et al., 2008.

claim: There is evidence that humans exhibit choice biases when only choosing between appetitive items.
source: However, there is some evidence that humans also exhibit choice biases when only choosing between appetitive items (Cavanagh et al., 2014; Smith and Krajbich, 2018; Smith and Krajbich, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cavanagh et al., 2014; Smith and Krajbich, 2018; Smith and Krajbich, 2019.

claim: Spreading a fixed cognitive reserve evenly between the attended and unattended items maximized performance.
source: Instead, spreading a fixed cognitive reserve evenly between the attended and unattended items maximized performance.
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations.

claim: A modified drift diffusion model with a continuously varying attention would perform optimally when attention is always equally divided.
source: This is consistent with prior work that showed that a modified drift diffusion model with a continuously varying attention would perform optimally when attention is always equally divided (Fudenberg et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fudenberg et al., 2018.

claim: Parameters fit to human behavior reveal that humans tend to allocate a large proportion of their cognitive resource toward the attended item.
source: Parameters fit to human behavior reveal that humans tend to allocate a large proportion of their cognitive resource toward the attended item, suggesting that the benefits of an attentional bottleneck might lie in other cognitive processes.
evidence: This is an inference from the parameter fitting results.

claim: Machine learning applied to text translation benefits from attentional bottlenecks.
source: Indeed, machine learning applied to text translation (Bahdanau et al., 2015; Gehring et al., 2017), object recognition (Mnih et al., 2014; Ba et al., 2015), and video-game playing (Sorokin et al., 2015) benefits from attentional bottlenecks that allow the algorithm to focus resources on specific task subcomponents.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bahdanau et al., 2015 and Gehring et al., 2017.

claim: Machine learning applied to object recognition benefits from attentional bottlenecks.
source: Indeed, machine learning applied to text translation (Bahdanau et al., 2015; Gehring et al., 2017), object recognition (Mnih et al., 2014; Ba et al., 2015), and video-game playing (Sorokin et al., 2015) benefits from attentional bottlenecks that allow the algorithm to focus resources on specific task subcomponents.
evidence: Supported by citations to Mnih et al., 2014 and Ba et al., 2015.

claim: Machine learning applied to video-game playing benefits from attentional bottlenecks.
source: Indeed, machine learning applied to text translation (Bahdanau et al., 2015; Gehring et al., 2017), object recognition (Mnih et al., 2014; Ba et al., 2015), and video-game playing (Sorokin et al., 2015) benefits from attentional bottlenecks that allow the algorithm to focus resources on specific task subcomponents.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sorokin et al., 2015.

claim: Image classification algorithms that extract only the relevant features of an image for high-resolution processing demonstrated improved performance and reduced computational cost compared to those without such attentional features.
source: For instance, image classification algorithms that extract only the relevant features of an image for high-resolution processing demonstrated improved performance and reduced computational cost compared to those without such attentional features (Mnih et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mnih et al., 2014.

claim: Attentional bottlenecks that appear to limit human decision-making performance might have beneficial effects on cognitive domains outside the scope of binary value-based decisions.
source: Similarly, attentional bottlenecks that appear to limit human decision-making performance might have beneficial effects on cognitive domains outside the scope of binary value-based decisions.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings.

claim: The evolutionary advantage of selective attention involves the ability to rapidly fixate on salient features in a cluttered environment, thereby limiting the amount of information that reaches upstream processing and reducing the overall computational burden.
source: This is consistent with the idea that the evolutionary advantage of selective attention involves the ability to rapidly fixate on salient features in a cluttered environment, thereby limiting the amount of information that reaches upstream processing and reducing the overall computational burden (Itti and Koch, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Itti and Koch, 2001.

claim: A choice bias driven by a zero-mean prior would generalize to decisions involving more than two options.
source: While implementing the optimal policy for such choices may be analytically intractable, we can reasonably infer that a choice bias driven by a zero-mean prior would generalize to decisions involving more than two options.
evidence: This is a speculation about generalization.

claim: In a multi-alternative choice paradigm where heuristics involving value and salience of items may influence attention allocation, it is less clear whether an equally divided attention among all options would still maximize reward.
source: However, in a multi-alternative choice paradigm where heuristics involving value and salience of items may influence attention allocation, it is less clear whether an equally divided attention among all options would still maximize reward.
evidence: This is a speculation about multi-alternative choices.
